metadata.summary: This guideline evaluates evidence for neurocritical care interventions in adults with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, both before and after the ruptured aneurysm is secured. It addresses prevention of rebleeding and delayed cerebral ischemia, fluid and hemodynamic management, and management of hyponatremia, anemia, and hydrocephalus. Using GRADE, it identifies interventions to use or avoid and clinical questions for which evidence remains insufficient.

therapeutic_areas: Blood pressure management for prevention of rebleeding
Antifibrinolytic therapy for prevention of rebleeding
Blood pressure and cardiac output augmentation
Triggers for interventional procedures to treat delayed cerebral ischemia
External ventricular drain removal strategies for hydrocephalus

conditions.name: aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH)
conditions.description: Subarachnoid hemorrhage caused by a ruptured aneurysm. The guideline addresses neurocritical care before and after the aneurysm is secured.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Acute hypertension may occur before the aneurysm is secured. Patients may subsequently develop rebleeding, delayed cerebral ischemia, hyponatremia, anemia, or hydrocephalus.

prognostic_tools.name: World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) grading scale
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Admission grade was used to adjust the analysis of 6-month mRS outcomes in the STASH trial; the guideline does not provide grade definitions.

risk_groups.criteria: The patient group studied by Egge et al.; individual grade criteria are not provided.

conditions.name: delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI)
conditions.description: An ischemic complication considered both for prevention after aSAH and for treatment when it develops.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptomatic cases may involve a change in neurological examination or neurological deficits.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a clinical change that could prompt consideration of an interventional procedure.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When DCI is suspected after aSAH.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evidence is insufficient to determine whether an examination change alone is a better intervention trigger than an examination change combined with advanced neuroimaging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide advanced neuroimaging findings considered alongside examination changes as a possible trigger for intervention.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating a patient for an interventional procedure for DCI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline does not establish whether adding neuroimaging findings improves selection for intervention.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide advanced neuroimaging findings considered alongside examination changes as a possible trigger for intervention.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating a patient for an interventional procedure for DCI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline does not establish whether adding neuroimaging findings improves selection for intervention.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide findings considered alongside examination changes as a possible trigger for intervention.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating a patient for an interventional procedure for DCI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline does not establish whether adding these findings improves selection for intervention.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify parameters associated with DCI in a cited study.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited study identified parameters sensitive and specific for DCI, but it did not resolve the guideline's question about intervention triggers.

conditions.name: hyponatremia
conditions.description: A complication after aSAH examined in studies of mineralocorticoids for prevention; the guideline states that studies testing mineralocorticoids to treat established hyponatremia are unavailable.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess sodium concentrations in studies of hyponatremia prevention.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The cited trials generally defined hyponatremia as serum sodium lower than 135 mEq/L on at least 2 consecutive days.

conditions.name: anemia
conditions.description: A potentially modifiable complication after aSAH that may influence secondary brain injury.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline describes anemia as common after aSAH but provides no frequency.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure concentrations used to evaluate transfusion strategies.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In studies comparing transfusion strategies for patients with aSAH.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline discusses strategies to maintain hemoglobin > 10 g/dL or > 7 g/dL, but does not define an anemia diagnostic threshold.

conditions.name: hydrocephalus
conditions.description: A complication of aSAH addressed through decisions about removal of an indwelling external ventricular drain (EVD) and possible ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess whether an EVD can be removed safely or a VP shunt is needed.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When considering EVD removal in a patient with aSAH and hydrocephalus.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline finds insufficient evidence to prefer direct clamping over gradual weaning.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess whether an EVD can be removed safely or a VP shunt is needed.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When considering EVD removal in a patient with aSAH and hydrocephalus.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline finds insufficient evidence to prefer gradual weaning over direct clamping.

toxicities.event: Increased mortality in older trials of long-term antifibrinolytic treatment

recognition: Reduced cerebral perfusion is a potential consequence.
toxicities.dose_modifications: In practice, associated hypotension may lead to splitting the dose to 30 mg every 2 h or stopping treatment. The effect of dose reduction or discontinuation on outcomes, compared with completing treatment at the standard dose, is unknown.

toxicities.incidence: At least one episode occurred in 34.5% of the IV nicardipine group versus 17.5% of the placebo group; severe life-threatening hypotension occurred in 3% in each arm.
These events occurred in 6.0% of the IV nicardipine group versus 2.4% of the placebo group (p < 0.001).

toxicities.event: Adverse events resulting in treatment termination
toxicities.incidence: Treatment was terminated because of adverse events in 14.1% of the IV nicardipine group versus 5.9% of the placebo group (p < 0.001).

toxicities.event: Pulmonary complications related to fluid retention
Pulmonary edema associated with liberal fluid administration
prevention: The guideline suggests avoiding liberal fluid administration because of this risk.

toxicities.event: Severe adverse events associated with induced hypertension
toxicities.incidence: Gathier et al. reported severe adverse events in 11% of patients treated with induced hypertension versus 5% of the comparison group (Relative risk 2.1; 95% CI 0.9–5.0).
recognition: Reported events included death, pneumothorax, atrial fibrillation, and myocardial infarction.
prevention: Use hemodynamic augmentation judiciously, tailor it to the patient's hemodynamic profile, and monitor closely for complications.

prophylaxis.type: Blood Pressure Targets for the Prevention of Rebleeding of Ruptured Aneurysm
prophylaxis.recommendation: Evidence is insufficient to specify a blood pressure reduction target for hypertension before aneurysm treatment in aSAH. This does not establish that reducing blood pressure before treatment is unhelpful.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with aSAH before treatment of the ruptured aneurysm

prophylaxis.type: Antifibrinolytics for the Prevention of Rebleeding of Ruptured Aneurysm
prophylaxis.recommendation: The guideline recommends against antifibrinolytic therapy to prevent rebleeding from a ruptured aneurysm.
The guideline recommends oral nimodipine to lower the occurrence of DCI and cerebral infarction and improve functional outcome.
prophylaxis.duration: 21 days was the treatment duration in all oral nimodipine RCTs; whether a shorter course is equally effective remains unresolved.

prophylaxis.recommendation: The guideline recommends against IV nicardipine for DCI prevention because adverse effects are more frequent.
Evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against calcium channel blockers other than nicardipine administered intravenously or intraventricularly.
The guideline recommends against endothelin receptor antagonist administration because it does not improve mortality or functional outcomes and increases adverse events.
The guideline recommends against initiating statin treatment to reduce DCI or improve functional outcomes. This recommendation does not address whether to continue a statin taken before admission.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with aSAH in whom statin treatment would be newly initiated

prophylaxis.recommendation: The guideline recommends against targeted hypermagnesemia to improve outcomes because benefit was lacking.
The guideline suggests against liberal fluid administration because it increases the risk of pulmonary edema.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with aSAH at risk for DCI

prophylaxis.recommendation: The guideline suggests targeted fluid administration to achieve euvolemia, potentially including goal-directed hemodynamic therapy, to lower pulmonary edema risk, prevent DCI, and improve functional outcome.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with aSAH at risk for DCI

prophylaxis.type: Hemodynamic Management: Blood Pressure and Cardiac Output Augmentation
prophylaxis.recommendation: Evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against blood pressure or cardiac output augmentation to prevent or treat DCI. Given the risks, any use should be judicious and individualized to the patient's hemodynamic profile.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with aSAH at risk for DCI or diagnosed with DCI

prophylaxis.type: Mineralocorticoid Therapy for the Management of Hyponatremia
prophylaxis.recommendation: Evidence is insufficient to support mineralocorticoid administration to maintain normal serum sodium concentrations or even fluid balance, or to improve functional outcome. Available studies assessed prevention rather than treatment of hyponatremia.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with hypertension before treatment of the ruptured aneurysm.
decision_rules: Evidence is insufficient to specify a blood pressure reduction target before aneurysm treatment.
The absence of an evidence-based target does not establish that lowering blood pressure is unhelpful.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Acute hypertension is usually treated before aneurysm securement, but no particular target has adequate evidence for preventing rebleeding or improving mortality or functional outcomes. Elevated systolic blood pressure, especially above 160 mm Hg, has been associated with rebleeding; this association is not a recommended treatment threshold. Whether reducing early blood pressure variability improves outcomes is unknown.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients before treatment of a ruptured aneurysm.
decision_rules: Do not administer antifibrinolytic therapy for prevention of rebleeding.

not_recommended.name: antifibrinolytic therapy
not_recommended.reason: Strong recommendation against its use for rebleeding prevention, with high-moderate quality of evidence. Clinical trials did not demonstrate improved long-term clinical outcomes, including with early, short-term treatment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Studies evaluated TXA and EACA over differing durations. In the ULTRA trial, ultra-early, short-term TXA did not improve functional outcome at 6 months; the trial also found no differences in rebleeding, mortality, cerebral ischemia or thromboembolic complications compared with placebo. Findings from studies of longer administration included reduced rebleeding in some studies but increased ischemic complications; these findings do not change the recommendation against antifibrinolytic therapy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with aSAH receiving prophylaxis against DCI.
decision_rules: Administer oral nimodipine to reduce DCI and cerebral infarction and improve functional outcome.
Do not use IV nicardipine to prevent DCI.
Evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against IV or intraventricular calcium channel blockers other than IV nicardipine.

recommended_regimens.name: oral nimodipine
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommended for patients with aSAH to prevent DCI and cerebral infarction and improve functional outcome. The most commonly used regimen is 60 mg every 4 h.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Studies reported improved functional outcome and reduced cerebral infarction or DCI; nimodipine appears to improve outcomes without significantly lowering angiographic vasospasm rates.

not_recommended.name: IV nicardipine
not_recommended.reason: Strong recommendation against its use for DCI prevention, with moderate quality of evidence: trials did not improve clinically relevant outcomes and showed increased adverse effects, including hypotension, pulmonary edema and acute renal insufficiency.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: All RCTs of oral nimodipine used 21 days. Trials also studied 90 mg every 4 h and 0.35 mg/kg every 4 h, but the guideline does not designate them as preferred alternatives. Hypotension may prompt dose splitting to 30 mg every 2 h or discontinuation in practice; whether dose reduction, splitting or interruption preserves benefit is unknown. Evidence does not establish that stopping after 14 days or at earlier hospital discharge is as effective as completing 21 days. For IV nicardipine, a study of 0.15 mg/ kg/hr for up to 14 days in 906 patients found hypotension in 34.5% of treated patients versus 17.5% with placebo; severe life-threatening hypotension occurred in 3% in each arm. Pulmonary edema and azotemia occurred in 6.0% versus 2.4% (p < 0.001), and treatment ended because of adverse events in 14.1% versus 5.9% (p < 0.001). Studies of other IV or intraventricular approaches had conflicting findings and low to very low quality of evidence.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considered for endothelin receptor antagonist administration.
decision_rules: Do not administer endothelin receptor antagonists for aSAH.

not_recommended.name: endothelin receptor antagonists
not_recommended.reason: Strong recommendation against their use, with high quality of evidence, because mortality and functional outcomes did not improve and adverse events increased.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In phase III trials, clasozentan was associated with adverse effects including fluid-retention-related pulmonary complications, hypotension and anemia. A 15 mg/ hr dose in CONSCIOUS-3 was associated with a significant reduction in the combined outcome of all-cause mortality and vasospasm-related morbidity at 6 weeks (OR 0.474; 95% CI 0.275–0.818; p = 0.0075), but not with improved extended GOS scores (OR 1.337; 95% CI 0.802–2.22; p = 0.266). These trial results do not change the recommendation against treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients in whom statin treatment would be newly initiated after aSAH.
decision_rules: Do not start statin treatment to reduce DCI or improve functional outcome.
The recommendation does not address whether to continue a statin already taken before admission.

not_recommended.name: statin treatment
not_recommended.reason: Strong recommendation against new initiation, with high quality of evidence: a large phase III RCT demonstrated lack of benefit for short-term and long-term outcomes in statin-naïve patients.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In STASH, 803 patients received simvastatin 40 mg/ day or placebo for up to 21 days; adjusted 6-month mRS scores did not differ (OR 0.97; 95% CIs 0.75–1.25). A trial comparing simvastatin 40 mg/day with 80 mg/day found no difference in DCI risk or 3-month functional outcome. Pitavastatin 4 mg daily reduced severe angiographic vasospasm in another trial without significantly reducing DCI or improving 3-month functional outcome.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considered for targeted therapeutic hypermagnesemia to improve outcomes.
decision_rules: Do not use targeted hypermagnesemia to improve outcomes after aSAH.

not_recommended.name: targeted hypermagnesemia
not_recommended.reason: Strong recommendation against its use, with moderate quality evidence, because larger phase III RCTs did not corroborate benefits suggested by preliminary studies.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Early studies assessed targets ranging from 2.0–2.5 mmol/L to twice baseline or 4–5.5 mg/dL; these are studied targets, not recommended goals. Two subsequent phase III trials included 327 and 1203 patients, respectively, and found no improvement in functional outcomes or death with IV magnesium sulfate infusion versus placebo.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients at risk for DCI who require fluid administration.
decision_rules: Avoid liberal fluid administration targeting hypervolemia because pulmonary edema risk is increased.
Use targeted fluid administration to achieve euvolemia; this may include goal-directed hemodynamic therapy.
No specific fluid-management or hemodynamic protocol has sufficient supporting evidence.

recommended_regimens.name: targeted fluid administration to achieve euvolemia
recommended_regimens.summary: Suggested fluid strategy; goal-directed hemodynamic therapy may be included to reduce pulmonary edema risk, prevent DCI and improve functional outcome.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Limited evidence suggests that protocolized management may reduce DCI and pulmonary edema and improve functional outcomes; a specific protocol is not established.

not_recommended.name: liberal fluid administration
not_recommended.reason: Conditional recommendation against its use, with low quality of evidence, because hypervolemic approaches showed a consistent increase in pulmonary edema without demonstrated benefit for DCI, cerebral infarction, mortality or functional outcomes.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The technique for assessing or achieving euvolemia remains undefined. Earlier comparisons suggesting benefit from more liberal fluids versus fluid restriction or diuresis were judged no longer applicable because practice changed over time. Individual studies did not find a statistically significant increase in pulmonary edema, although the signal was consistent across hypervolemic arms.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients at risk for DCI or diagnosed with DCI.
decision_rules: Evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against augmentation of blood pressure or cardiac output for DCI prevention or treatment.
If these interventions are used, apply them judiciously according to the patient's individual hemodynamic profile and monitor for complications.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The conclusion reflects a lack of adequate supporting studies, not proof that hemodynamic augmentation has no benefit. The guidance does not select individual pharmacological agents. Reviewed studies reported cardiovascular adverse events; in a study of induced hypertension, severe adverse events occurred in 11% versus 5% (Relative risk 2.1; 95% CI 0.9–5.0). Studies of IV milrinone were inconclusive.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients being assessed for interventional procedures to treat DCI.
decision_rules: Evidence is insufficient to select neurological examination changes alone or examination changes combined with advanced neuroimaging findings as the preferred trigger for intervention.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No formal study compared these approaches as triggers for intervention. The advanced assessments considered in the clinical question were Computed Tomography (CT) Angiography, CT Perfusion and transcranial Doppler; the guideline does not establish a preferred trigger.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considered for mineralocorticoids to maintain serum sodium concentrations or fluid balance, or to improve functional outcome.
decision_rules: Evidence is insufficient to support mineralocorticoid administration for these purposes.
Studies of hyponatremia prevention must not be taken as evidence for treating established hyponatremia.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Trials assessed fludrocortisone or hydrocortisone started within 48–72 h of aSAH onset and continued for 10–14 days, but did not test treatment of established hyponatremia. They suggested less hyponatremia and natriuresis without improved DCI or functional outcomes; the evidence was inconclusive and hypokalemia was more common with mineralocorticoids. No evidence establishes improved functional outcome from their use.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with aSAH being considered for red blood cell transfusion.
decision_rules: Evidence is insufficient to recommend a transfusion threshold higher than a hemoglobin of > 7 g/dL.
No optimal transfusion strategy or hemoglobin threshold specific to aSAH has been established.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The clinical question compared strategies maintaining hemoglobin > 10 g/dL and > 7 g/dL; neither was established as preferable. A small RCT comparing goals of at least 10 g/dL and 11.5 g/dL within 3 days of aSAH onset found no difference in new cerebral infarction, DCI prevention or transfusion-related complications. These study results do not establish a transfusion threshold.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with hydrocephalus and an indwelling external ventricular drain (EVD) being assessed for drain removal.
decision_rules: Evidence is insufficient to recommend direct clamping over gradual weaning, or the reverse, for EVD removal.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The strategies have not been adequately compared, so the optimal EVD removal approach remains unknown. In a single-center RCT of 81 patients, VP shunting occurred in 63.4% with direct clamping versus 62.5% with gradual weaning over 3 days; direct clamping shortened EVD duration and intensive care unit stay, with comparable safety. An observational comparison combining intermittent CSF drainage with rapid weaning found VP shunting in 13% versus 35% with continuous drainage and gradual weaning; its combined strategies do not isolate the effect of weaning speed. A prospective multicenter observational study of 139 patients found a nonsignificant adjusted trend toward fewer VP shunts with rapid versus gradual weaning (OR 0.43; 95% CI 0.18–1.03).

therapies_index.name: antifibrinolytic therapy
therapies_index.administration: Studied before aneurysm treatment to prevent rebleeding in aSAH, both throughout hospitalization for up to 4 weeks and for less than 72 h. The guideline recommends against this use.
key_toxicities: Cerebral ischemic deficits and thromboembolic complications were reported in studies of antifibrinolytic treatment.

therapies_index.name: tranexamic acid
therapies_index.administration: Studied for prevention of rebleeding as treatment throughout hospitalization for up to 4 weeks or as treatment lasting less than 72 h; the guideline recommends against antifibrinolytic therapy for this purpose.
key_toxicities: Most older RCTs of prolonged TXA treatment reported increased cerebral ischemic complications and mortality.

therapies_index.name: ε-aminocaproic acid
therapies_index.administration: Studied as prolonged antifibrinolytic treatment and in shorter courses for prevention of rebleeding; the guideline recommends against antifibrinolytic therapy for this purpose.
key_toxicities: Two studies of shorter EACA treatment associated it with increased thromboembolic complications. Studies of prolonged antifibrinolytic treatment that included EACA reported more cerebral ischemic deficits.

therapies_index.name: nimodipine
approved_indications: The guideline recommends oral administration in aSAH to reduce DCI and cerebral infarction and improve functional outcome.
therapies_index.administration: The oral regimen most commonly used is 60 mg every 4 h for 21 days. Other RCT regimens were 90 mg every 4 h and 0.35 mg/kg every 4 h; all oral RCTs treated for 21 days. A split regimen of 30 mg every 2 h is described in practice when hypotension occurs. Continuous IV administration, including use followed by oral nimodipine, and single-dose intraventricular sustained-release microparticles were also studied, without an established recommendation for these routes.
key_toxicities: Hypotension with oral nimodipine may reduce cerebral perfusion.

therapies_index.name: nicardipine
therapies_index.administration: Continuous IV nicardipine was studied at 0.15 mg/ kg/hr for up to 14 days to prevent DCI; the guideline recommends against IV use for this purpose. Intraventricular administration and prolonged-release implants were also studied, but the evidence was insufficient to recommend their prophylactic use.
key_toxicities: In the continuous IV nicardipine study, hypotension occurred in 34.5% of treated patients versus 17.5% with placebo; severe life-threatening hypotension occurred in 3% in each arm.
Pulmonary edema and azotemia occurred in 6.0% of the IV nicardipine group versus 2.4% of the placebo group (p < 0.001).
Treatment was stopped because of adverse events in 14.1% of the IV nicardipine group versus 5.9% of the placebo group (p < 0.001).

therapies_index.name: flunarizine
therapies_index.administration: Oral administration was evaluated in a study of prophylactic calcium channel blockers; the guideline gives no recommendation specific to flunarizine.

therapies_index.name: clazosentan
therapies_index.administration: Studied as an endothelin receptor antagonist in aSAH. CONSCIOUS-3 studied a higher dosage of 15 mg/ hr. The guideline recommends against endothelin receptor antagonist administration.
key_toxicities: Phase III studies of endothelin receptor antagonists reported pulmonary complications related to fluid retention, hypotension and anemia.

therapies_index.name: statin treatment
therapies_index.administration: The guideline recommends against newly starting treatment to reduce DCI or improve functional outcome in aSAH; it does not address continuation of treatment begun before admission.

therapies_index.name: pravastatin
therapies_index.administration: Studied when started within 48–72 h of aSAH onset; the guideline recommends against starting statin treatment to reduce DCI or improve functional outcome.

therapies_index.name: simvastatin
therapies_index.administration: In STASH, 40 mg/ day was administered for up to 21 days to patients presenting within 96 h of aSAH. Another RCT compared 40 mg/day with 80 mg/day. The guideline recommends against starting statin treatment to reduce DCI or improve functional outcome.

therapies_index.name: pitavastatin
therapies_index.administration: Studied at 4 mg daily; the guideline recommends against starting statin treatment to reduce DCI or improve functional outcome.

therapies_index.name: targeted hypermagnesemia
therapies_index.administration: Studies used fixed or weight-based dosing, or targeted serum concentrations ranging from high-normal (2.0–2.5 mmol/L) to supratherapeutic (twice baseline or a goal magnesium concentration of 4–5.5 mg/dL). The guideline recommends against its use to improve aSAH outcomes.
monitoring: Serum magnesium concentrations were treatment targets in some studies.

therapies_index.name: magnesium sulfate
therapies_index.administration: IV infusion was studied in phase III trials for aSAH. The guideline recommends against targeted hypermagnesemia to improve outcomes.

therapies_index.name: liberal fluid administration
therapies_index.administration: High-volume administration targeting hypervolemia was studied in patients with aSAH at risk for DCI. The guideline suggests against this strategy.
key_toxicities: Pulmonary edema was consistently more frequent with liberal or hypervolemic strategies than with conventional management targeting euvolemia, although the increase was not statistically significant in any individual study.

therapies_index.name: targeted fluid administration
approved_indications: The guideline suggests administration aimed at euvolemia to reduce pulmonary edema risk, prevent DCI and improve functional outcome in aSAH.
therapies_index.administration: May include goal-directed hemodynamic therapy; the guideline does not specify a fluid protocol.
monitoring: Assessment of euvolemia is discussed, but no preferred assessment technique is established.

therapies_index.name: goal-directed hemodynamic therapy
approved_indications: The guideline says this approach may be included in targeted fluid administration aimed at euvolemia in aSAH.
therapies_index.administration: Studied in protocols using transpulmonary thermodilution to guide fluid and cardiovascular treatment; the guideline does not recommend a specific protocol.
monitoring: Transpulmonary thermodilution was used for hemodynamic assessment in studied protocols.

therapies_index.name: EGDT
therapies_index.administration: Studied as an early goal-directed fluid therapy algorithm based on transpulmonary thermodilution and in protocols guiding care before and after DCI symptoms.
monitoring: Studied protocols used a central line and noninvasive or invasive cardiac output monitoring; one fluid-therapy algorithm used transpulmonary thermodilution.

therapies_index.name: fluid restriction
therapies_index.administration: Compared with more liberal fluid administration in early studies; the guideline does not recommend it as a specific strategy.

therapies_index.name: diuresis
therapies_index.administration: Compared with more liberal fluid administration in early studies; the guideline does not recommend it as a specific strategy.

therapies_index.name: blood pressure reduction
therapies_index.administration: Acute hypertension is usually treated before aneurysm securement, but evidence is insufficient to recommend a specific blood pressure reduction goal in aSAH.

therapies_index.name: blood pressure augmentation
therapies_index.administration: Studied for prevention and treatment of DCI. Evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against it; the guideline says use should be judicious and tailored to the individual hemodynamic profile.
key_toxicities: Studies reported an association between blood pressure augmentation and cardiovascular adverse events.

therapies_index.name: cardiac output augmentation
therapies_index.administration: Studied for prevention and treatment of DCI. Evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against it; the guideline says use should be judicious and tailored to the individual hemodynamic profile.
key_toxicities: Studies reported an association between cardiac augmentation and cardiovascular adverse events.

therapies_index.name: induced hypertension
therapies_index.administration: Studied to prevent DCI and to treat symptomatic DCI. In one RCT, fluids and norepinephrine were continued until neurological deficits improved, a maximum systolic/mean arterial pressure of 230/130 mm Hg was reached, or a complication occurred. The guideline does not recommend a specific augmentation strategy.
key_toxicities: In one prevention study, patients had worse neurobehavioral scores and some developed significant adverse events, including pulmonary edema.

In a treatment study, severe adverse events occurred in 11% with induced hypertension versus 5% in the comparison group (Relative risk 2.1; 95% CI 0.9–5.0), including death, pneumothorax, atrial fibrillation and myocardial infarction.
monitoring: Neurological deficits and blood pressure were treatment endpoints in one RCT.

therapies_index.name: norepinephrine
therapies_index.administration: Used with fluids to induce hypertension in a study of symptomatic DCI; another study compared norepinephrine-induced hypertension with dobutamine-induced cardiac index augmentation. The guideline does not recommend an individual agent.

therapies_index.name: dobutamine
therapies_index.administration: Studied for cardiac index augmentation in comparison with norepinephrine-induced hypertension. The guideline does not recommend an individual agent.

therapies_index.name: milrinone
therapies_index.administration: Studies compared IV with IV+ IA administration and IV administration with continuous magnesium infusion for 21 days. The findings were inconclusive.

therapies_index.name: fludrocortisone
therapies_index.administration: Studied for prevention of hyponatremia and volume contraction when started within 48–72 h of aSAH onset and continued for 10–14 days. The guideline finds insufficient evidence to support mineralocorticoid administration for its stated outcomes.
key_toxicities: Hypokalemia was more common among patients receiving mineralocorticoids in the studies reviewed.
monitoring: Studied outcomes included serum sodium concentrations and fluid balance.

therapies_index.name: hydrocortisone
therapies_index.administration: Studied for prevention of hyponatremia and volume contraction when started within 48–72 h of aSAH onset and continued for 10–14 days. The guideline finds insufficient evidence to support mineralocorticoid administration for its stated outcomes.
key_toxicities: Hypokalemia was more common among patients receiving mineralocorticoids in the studies reviewed.
monitoring: Studied outcomes included serum sodium concentrations and fluid balance.

therapies_index.name: red blood cell transfusion
therapies_index.administration: Studies compared strategies intended to maintain hemoglobin > 10 g/dL or > 7 g/dL; another RCT studied goals of at least 10 g/dL or 11.5 g/dL within 3 days of aSAH onset. Evidence is insufficient to recommend a transfusion threshold higher than a hemoglobin of > 7 g/dL.
monitoring: Hemoglobin concentration was used to define the studied transfusion goals.

therapies_index.name: surgical clipping
therapies_index.administration: Described as a method of treating the ruptured aneurysm; a phase III clasozentan study enrolled patients undergoing surgical clipping.

therapies_index.name: endovascular coiling

recommendations.statement: The evidence is insufficient to specify a blood pressure reduction target when treating hypertension before aneurysm treatment in aSAH. This does not establish that lowering blood pressure is unhelpful.
recommendations.context: Before treatment of the ruptured aneurysm.
recommendations.rationale: The available comparisons are too limited to establish a target; the studies included some treatment of severe hypertension.
recommendations.source_heading: Blood Pressure Targets for the Prevention of Rebleeding of Ruptured Aneurysm

recommendations.statement: Do not administer antifibrinolytic therapy to prevent rebleeding from a ruptured aneurysm in patients with aSAH.
recommendations.context: Prevention of rebleeding before aneurysm treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Well-designed trials did not show improved long-term clinical outcomes; subsequent trials did not confirm the earlier suggested protection against rebleeding.
recommendations.source_heading: Antifibrinolytics for the Prevention of Rebleeding of Ruptured Aneurysm

recommendations.statement: Administer oral nimodipine to patients with aSAH to lower the occurrence of DCI and cerebral infarction and improve functional outcome.
recommendations.context: Prophylactic administration of calcium channel blockers.
recommendations.rationale: Studies of oral nimodipine showed better functional outcomes and lower rates of DCI or infarction.

recommendations.statement: Do not administer intravenous (IV) nicardipine to prevent DCI because it increases adverse effects.
recommendations.context: Prophylactic administration in patients with aSAH.
recommendations.rationale: Trials found no improvement in clinically relevant outcomes and identified increased risks of hypotension, pulmonary edema and acute renal insufficiency.

recommendations.statement: The evidence is insufficient to favor or oppose intravenous or intraventricular administration of calcium channel blockers other than nicardipine.
recommendations.context: Prophylactic administration in patients with aSAH.
recommendations.rationale: Studies of other agents and routes were of insufficient quality and yielded conflicting results.

recommendations.statement: Do not administer endothelin receptor antagonists to patients with aSAH: they do not improve mortality or functional outcomes and increase adverse events.
recommendations.context: Pharmacological intervention in patients with aSAH.
recommendations.rationale: Phase III trials found no improvement in functional outcomes and identified notable adverse effects.

recommendations.statement: Do not initiate statin treatment in aSAH to reduce DCI or improve functional outcomes, because it provides no benefit for these purposes.
recommendations.context: Initiation of treatment; this recommendation does not address continuation in patients already taking a statin before admission.
recommendations.rationale: A large phase III trial demonstrated no short-term or long-term outcome benefit from starting statins in statin-naïve patients.

recommendations.statement: Do not use targeted hypermagnesemia to improve outcomes in aSAH, because it has not provided benefit.
recommendations.context: Therapeutic hypermagnesemia in patients with aSAH.
recommendations.rationale: Larger randomized trials did not confirm the possible benefits suggested by earlier pilot studies.

recommendations.statement: Avoid liberal fluid administration because it raises the risk of pulmonary edema.
recommendations.context: Fluid management in patients with aSAH at risk for DCI.
recommendations.rationale: Liberal administration targeting hypervolemia showed no supported benefit for neurological outcomes, while pulmonary edema occurred more often than with management targeting euvolemia.

recommendations.statement: Use targeted fluid administration to achieve euvolemia; this may include goal-directed hemodynamic therapy, with the aims of lowering pulmonary edema risk, preventing DCI and improving functional outcome.
recommendations.context: Fluid management in patients with aSAH at risk for DCI.
recommendations.rationale: Limited evidence suggests that protocolized fluid management may achieve euvolemia and improve these outcomes.

recommendations.statement: Evidence of sufficient quality is lacking to recommend for or against augmenting blood pressure or cardiac output to prevent or treat DCI. If these interventions are used, apply them judiciously according to the patient's individual hemodynamic profile.
recommendations.context: Patients with aSAH at risk for DCI or diagnosed with DCI.
recommendations.rationale: Existing studies do not adequately establish benefit or rule it out, and hemodynamic augmentation carries risks.
recommendations.source_heading: Hemodynamic Management: Blood Pressure and Cardiac Output Augmentation

recommendations.statement: The evidence is insufficient to determine whether interventional treatment of DCI should be triggered by a neurological examination change together with advanced neuroimaging findings or by the examination change alone.
recommendations.context: Selection of patients with aSAH for interventional procedures to treat DCI.
recommendations.rationale: No formal study compared these two approaches to triggering intervention.
recommendations.source_heading: DCI Management: Triggers for Interventional Procedures for Treatment of DCI

recommendations.statement: The evidence is insufficient to support administering mineralocorticoids to maintain normal serum sodium, maintain even fluid balance or improve functional outcome.
recommendations.context: Management of hyponatremia in patients with aSAH.
recommendations.rationale: The available studies evaluated prevention rather than treatment of hyponatremia and were of insufficient quality to support mineralocorticoid use.
recommendations.source_heading: Mineralocorticoid Therapy for the Management of Hyponatremia

recommendations.statement: The evidence is insufficient to recommend a transfusion threshold higher than a hemoglobin of > 7 g/dL for patients with aSAH.
recommendations.rationale: Quality data assessing higher transfusion thresholds specifically in patients with aSAH are scarce.

recommendations.statement: The evidence is insufficient to recommend direct clamping over gradual weaning, or the reverse, when removing an EVD to manage hydrocephalus in patients with aSAH.
recommendations.context: Patients with aSAH and an indwelling EVD.
recommendations.rationale: The two EVD removal strategies have not been compared adequately, leaving the optimal approach uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Neurointensive management of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) influences outcomes in both the short and long term. This guideline updates recommendations developed after a 2011 consensus conference, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation methodology. Panel members selected and prioritized Population/Intervention/Comparator/Outcome (PICO) questions and their clinically relevant outcomes by consensus and survey. Eligible human research comprised randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective or retrospective observational studies, case–control studies, case series involving more than 20 patients, and meta-analyses. Reviewers screened titles, abstracts, and selected full texts; extracted eligible data in duplicate; assessed bias with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation tool for RCTs and the Risk of Bias In Nonrandomized Studies – of Interventions tool for observational research; and voted after discussing each evidence summary. The search found 15,107 unique publications, of which 74 underwent data abstraction. Several RCTs assessed drugs, whereas evidence addressing nonpharmacological questions was consistently poor. Five PICO questions yielded strong recommendations, one yielded conditional recommendations, and six lacked sufficient evidence for a recommendation. The guideline identifies supported interventions and evidence gaps; important management questions remain unresolved despite improving outcomes over time.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Neurointensive care is an important determinant of short-term and long-term outcomes after aSAH. Earlier guidance arose from a literature review and international expert consensus and was intended to support consistent decisions by multidisciplinary teams. Recent reports suggest meaningful functional improvement even among patients presenting with poor grade aSAH; improved surgical and endovascular techniques and broader advances in critical care are possible contributors. The Neurocritical Care Society convened a committee to update recommendations using the evolved Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. The selected topics were blood pressure before aneurysm securement, antifibrinolytics, calcium channel blockers, endothelin antagonists, statins, high dose magnesium, fluid and hemodynamic management, triggers for intervention in delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI), hyponatremia, anemia, and hydrocephalus. The guidance does not apply to children or people with nonaneurysmal SAH.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: Evidence assessment and guideline development followed the GRADE approach.

document_sections.heading: Panel Composition
document_sections.content: The panel assembled in March 2019 with 12 neurocritical care experts spanning neurology, anesthesiology, critical care, neurosurgery, and pharmacology. It also included experienced guideline methodologists and international representation. The Neurocritical Care Society supplied support for searching, reference management, and methodology.

document_sections.heading: Question Generation
document_sections.content: Panel consensus prioritized clinical questions framed as Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes (PICO). The guideline was not intended to cover every aspect of care: before searching, the panel planned to select up to ten questions from a broader topic list. Selection emphasized common critical-care interventions, particularly those with new evidence, while considering the subjects of the earlier guideline. Nine questions addressed both the immediate period before aneurysm securement and subsequent management; general neurocritical-care topics were excluded. Two members reviewed each question. The pharmacological DCI question was ultimately divided into calcium channel blockers, endothelin antagonists, statins, and magnesium.

document_sections.heading: Determination of Relevant Outcomes
document_sections.content: The panel sought clinically relevant and long-term outcomes beyond mortality. For every PICO question, members scored candidate outcomes on a survey ranging from “Critically Important” (score 9) to “Not Important” (score 1). After discussion, they retained outcomes with a median score higher than 5 or those accepted by agreement.

document_sections.heading: Search Strategy
document_sections.content: For each PICO question, its two reviewers refined its scope, proposed search terms, and identified two to three particularly relevant publications. A librarian searched Medline/PubMed, CINAHL, COCHRANE, and Embase for publications dating from 1946. Searches occurred on September 25, 2019, with an update on April 1, 2021. The initial search identified 15,107 unique publications.

document_sections.heading: Screening and Study Selection
document_sections.content: DistillerSR supported title-and-abstract screening at level 1, full-text assessment at level 2, and data abstraction at level 3. Eligible publications were in English, involved adults (> age 18), concerned human participants, and were peer reviewed. Eligible designs were RCTs, prospective or retrospective observational studies, case–control studies, case series with a sample larger than 20 patients, and meta-analyses. There was no publication-date restriction. Case reports, abstracts alone, and supplement-only reports were excluded. Full publications were assigned to relevant PICO topics before abstraction and could inform more than one question. The selection diagram shows 15,135 database records, 0 additional records, 15,107 records after deduplication, 13,961 records excluded at screening, 1,135 full-text articles assessed, 1,061 full-text articles excluded, and 74 studies in the qualitative synthesis.

document_sections.heading: Data Abstraction
document_sections.content: Two panel members assessed each study using a standardized abstraction and bias-appraisal database. They used the GRADE risk-of-bias tool for RCTs and Risk Of Bias In Non-Randomized Studies - of Interventions (ROBINS I) for observational studies. The full panel discussed discrepancies and uncertainties until a majority consensus was reached. Evidence summaries considered potential confounders.

document_sections.heading: Risk of Bias and Quality of the Evidence
document_sections.content: Overall evidence quality reflected risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, potential publication bias, and other limitations. Under GRADE, these considerations could raise or lower certainty.

document_sections.heading: Panel Discussion and Evidence to Recommendation Process
document_sections.content: After duplicate abstraction, the panel reviewed each PICO evidence summary, resolved questions, drafted a recommendation, and voted. Approval required agreement by greater than 80% of members. Initial disagreement arose only for calcium channel blockers; the panel separated that question by agent and administration route and then reached consensus. Evidence tables present the reviewed findings. Besides evidence quality, decisions considered certainty about benefits and harms and their balance for prespecified outcomes. GRADE labels were “strong,” “conditional,” and “insufficient evidence”: “we recommend” and “we recommend against” denote strong recommendations, whereas “we suggest” denotes conditional recommendations. The panel chose not to add good-practice statements based on minimal or absent evidence; its recommendations were not founded solely on personal opinion.

document_sections.heading: Summary of Recommendations
document_sections.content: Table 1 presents the recommendations across the PICO topics. It distinguishes interventions recommended, interventions advised against, conditional fluid-management suggestions, and questions for which evidence does not support a recommendation. Its markers identify recommendations changed from 2011 and subjects not addressed in the 2011 recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Blood Pressure Targets for the Prevention of Rebleeding of Ruptured Aneurysm PICO Question
document_sections.content: The question compares blood pressure reduction with no reduction before aneurysm treatment in aSAH, considering mortality, modified Rankin scale (mRS), Glasgow outcome scale (GOS), new cerebral infarction, rebleeding, and DCI. Table 2 summarizes the GRADE evidence profile. Evidence is insufficient to recommend a blood pressure reduction goal when treating hypertension before aneurysm treatment; this does not establish that reduction is unhelpful. The panel judged the available evidence too weak to select a target or favor reduction over no reduction, and every included study treated severe hypertension to some degree. Evidence on targets and functional outcome is retrospective or observational. Reports associate elevated systolic pressure, particularly above 160 mm Hg, with rebleeding. Lower pressure within one treatment protocol was associated with lower rebleeding odds, but the finding was not consistent across studies. A mixed neurocritical-care cohort did not substantiate concern that lowering pressure produces ischemia through impaired cerebral perfusion. Some evidence links greater blood pressure variability to rebleeding and worse outcomes; its role requires further study. Acute hypertension is usually treated until aneurysm securement, but no specific target has adequate evidentiary support for preventing rebleeding or improving mortality or function. Early variability may influence function, while the effect of reducing variability remains unknown. Further research must establish the optimal presecurement approach.

document_sections.heading: Antifibrinolytics for the Prevention of Rebleeding of Ruptured Aneurysm PICO Question
document_sections.content: The question examines antifibrinolytics before aneurysm treatment versus none for mortality, mRS, GOS, new infarction, rebleeding, DCI, and thrombosis. Table 3 gives the GRADE evidence profile. The panel advises against antifibrinolytic therapy to prevent ruptured-aneurysm rebleeding in aSAH (strong recommendation, high-moderate quality of evidence). Although rebleeding increases poor outcomes and mortality, well-designed trials did not demonstrate a long-term clinical benefit from its prevention with these agents. Earlier suggestions of protection were not confirmed by subsequent RCTs, prompting a change from the 2011 guidance. The review identified six RCTs, six observational studies, and 47 outcome analyses. Every RCT compared tranexamic acid (TXA) with placebo; non-RCT comparisons involved ε-aminocaproic acid (EACA), TXA, or both against no corresponding treatment. Older studies assessed treatment throughout admission and for up to 4 weeks; newer studies assessed courses of less than 72 h. Among four older TXA RCTs, three reported significantly less rebleeding and one reported no difference, while none found better functional outcomes; most reported more cerebral ischemic complications and mortality with TXA. Two non-RCTs of prolonged EACA found less rebleeding but more cerebral ischemic deficits. Of four observational studies of shorter therapy, two associated EACA with less rebleeding and more thromboembolism, another found no association, and the most recent associated early short-course TXA with lower mortality but not better function. One of two short-course TXA RCTs found less ultraearly rebleeding but lacked power to assess clinical outcomes. The largest, ULTRA, found no improvement in function at 6 months with ultra-early short-term TXA and no differences in rebleeding, mortality, cerebral ischemia, or thromboembolism versus placebo; excellent functional outcome was less likely in its TXA arm. In light of the full evidence, including an additional phase III trial, the panel unanimously replaced the earlier weak suggestion to consider an early short course with a recommendation against antifibrinolytics for this purpose.

document_sections.heading: Calcium Channel Blockers PICO Question
document_sections.content: This question assesses calcium channel blockers versus none for mortality, mRS, GOS, new cerebral infarction, and DCI prevention. Table 4 profiles evidence from eight RCTs and nine observational studies of prophylactic use; studies treating established DCI or angiographic vasospasm were excluded. The panel recommends oral nimodipine for patients with aSAH to reduce DCI and cerebral infarction and improve function (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence). Oral nimodipine is the only assessed agent shown to improve outcomes with high-quality evidence. Among five placebo comparisons, two showed improved 3-month GOS and, respectively, less infarction or DCI; another found significantly less DCI. A 2007 Cochrane Review supported these findings. Outcome improvement appeared without a significant decrease in angiographic vasospasm. The most commonly used oral schedule is 60 mg every 4 h for 21 days; other RCT schedules were 90 mg every 4 h and 0.35 mg/kg every 4 h. Hypotension can reduce cerebral perfusion and potentially offset benefit. Trial protocols often excluded patients who missed multiple doses, and hypotension was seldom reported; in practice it can prompt splitting to 30 mg every 2 h or stopping treatment. Retrospective links between altered schedules and poor outcomes are heavily confounded because withholding often coincided with DCI or vasospasm diagnosis and vasopressor initiation. The effects of reduction, interruption, or withholding during hypotension or blood pressure augmentation remain unknown. All oral RCTs treated for 21 days. Small retrospective reports suggest stopping after 14 days, or at earlier discharge than day 21, might not worsen outcomes, but equivalent effectiveness to 21 days has not been established. The panel recommends against intravenous (IV) nicardipine for DCI prevention because adverse effects increase (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence). Adequately powered trials yielded at most marginal intermediate-outcome improvement without meaningful clinical benefit and showed significantly greater adverse-effect risk. In a placebo comparison involving 906 patients, continuous IV nicardipine at 0.15 mg/ kg/hr for up to 14 days reduced symptomatic vasospasm without improving overall function. Hypotension occurred in 34.5% of its recipients versus 17.5% with placebo; severe life-threatening hypotension occurred in 3% in each arm. Pulmonary edema and azotemia occurred in 6.0% versus 2.4% (p < 0.001), and adverse events led to treatment termination in 14.1% versus 5.9% (p < 0.001). Evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against IV or intraventricular calcium channel blockers other than the excluded IV nicardipine approach. Ten additional studies evaluated continuous IV nimodipine alone, IV nimodipine followed by oral nimodipine, intraventricular nicardipine, or nicardipine prolonged-release implants; their low to very low quality and conflicting results preclude a recommendation. IV administration may increase hypotension or pulmonary edema. A separate RCT of single-dose intraventricular sustained-release nimodipine microparticles ended early for futility and was excluded because its comparator was oral nimodipine rather than placebo. Optimal handling of hemodynamic intolerance or concurrent vasopressors, and the effectiveness of abbreviated oral courses, remain unresolved.

document_sections.heading: Endothelin Antagonists PICO Question
document_sections.content: The question concerns endothelin antagonists versus no antagonists for mortality, mRS, GOS, new infarction, and DCI prevention; Table 5 summarizes certainty. The panel recommends against endothelin receptor antagonists because they do not benefit mortality or functional outcomes and increase adverse events (strong recommendation, high quality of evidence). Of six analyzed studies, four were dose-finding or phase II trials without power to establish efficacy; signals in their primary endpoints were not statistically significant. Subsequent phase III trials did not significantly improve mortality, mRS, GOS, new infarction, or DCI prevention. Among surgically clipped patients in CONSCIOUS-2, the relative risk reduction for vasospasm-related morbidity and all-cause mortality was 17% (95% confidence interval [CI]− 4 to 33; p = 0.10), which was not statistically significant. These results prompted early termination of CONSCIOUS-3, involving endovascular coiling. In CONSCIOUS-3, clasozentan at 15 mg/ hr significantly reduced all-cause mortality and vasospasm-related morbidity at 6 weeks (odds ratio [OR] 0.474; 95% CI 0.275–0.818; p = 0.0075), without improving extended GOS (OR 1.337; 95% CI 0.802–2.22; p = 0.266). Phase III adverse effects commonly included fluid-retention-related pulmonary complications, hypotension, and anemia. Favorable surrogate endpoints might justify future trials, but current evidence supports avoiding these antagonists.

document_sections.heading: Statins PICO Question
document_sections.content: This question assesses statins versus no statins for mortality, mRS, GOS, new infarction, and DCI prevention; Table 6 profiles the evidence. The panel recommends against starting statins to reduce DCI or improve functional outcomes in aSAH because benefit is absent (strong recommendation, high quality of evidence). This applies to newly initiated treatment, not to deciding whether to continue a statin taken before admission. The review found eight RCTs and six observational studies. Early, small RCTs with high Risk of Bias (ROB) suggested less vasospasm after pravastatin or simvastatin begun within 48–72 h of onset. A subsequent phase II trial did not confirm this, and historical-control comparisons of routine statin use found no outcome difference. The multicenter, double-blind STASH RCT allocated 803 patients presenting within 96 h to simvastatin 40 mg/ day or placebo for up to 21 days. Age- and admission World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS)-adjusted ordinal analysis of 6-month mRS showed no group difference (OR 0.97; 95% CIs 0.75–1.25). In-hospital mortality, DCI, rescue-treated DCI, radiological infarction, admission duration, and quality of life were likewise similar. A smaller RCT found no DCI or 3-month functional difference between simvastatin 40 mg/day and 80 mg/day. Another randomized trial associated pitavastatin 4 mg daily with less severe angiographic vasospasm, but not significantly less DCI or improved 3-month function. The adequately powered phase III evidence demonstrates no short-term or long-term outcome benefit from newly administering statins to statin-naïve patients.

document_sections.heading: Magnesium/Therapeutic Hypermagnesemia PICO Question
document_sections.content: The question compares targeted therapeutic hypermagnesemia with no such targeting for mortality, mRS, GOS, new infarction, and DCI prevention; Table 7 presents the evidence profile. The panel recommends against targeted hypermagnesemia to improve aSAH outcomes because benefit is absent (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). Early pilot regimens varied between fixed doses, weight-based doses, and serum targets from high-normal (2.0–2.5 mmol/L) to supratherapeutic concentrations (twice baseline or 4–5.5 mg/dL). Six phase II RCTs conducted between 2002 and 2010 suggested improvement but varied in dose and outcomes; contemporaneous observational findings were inconsistent and methodologically limited. Two later, large, saline-controlled phase III trials enrolled 327 and 1203 patients, respectively, and found no improvement in function or death with IV magnesium sulfate. A post hoc analysis of magnesium and glucose levels likewise found no magnesium benefit. Three further small studies, each involving ≤ 120 participants and varying dose, comparator, or concomitant medicines, gave mixed results but had substantial bias and methodological limitations. Phase III evidence did not show improvement in mortality, function, DCI, or cerebral infarction.

document_sections.heading: Hemodynamic Management: Fluid Administration PICO Question
document_sections.content: This question compares liberal, high-volume fluid administration targeting hypervolemia with conventional management targeting euvolemia in patients at risk of DCI, assessing mortality, mRS, GOS, infarction, DCI, and pulmonary edema. Table 8 profiles evidence from 14 studies. The panel suggests against liberal fluid administration because pulmonary edema risk increases (Conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence). Available literature does not support improved DCI, infarction, mortality, or function with liberal fluids, whereas pulmonary edema was consistently more frequent with hypervolemia than with euvolemic conventional care; individual-study increases were not statistically significant. The panel also suggests targeted fluid administration to achieve euvolemia, potentially including goal-directed hemodynamic therapy, to lower pulmonary edema risk, prevent DCI, and improve function (conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence). Limited evidence suggests protocolized approaches may achieve euvolemia and these outcomes. Three early studies favored liberal fluids over restriction or diuresis, but subsequent changes in practice make their findings inapplicable; aneurysm surgery was delayed for 7–10 days in the small randomized trial, while surgical timing was unspecified in the two observational studies. Four additional RCTs and two observational studies comparing hypervolemia with normovolemia or moderate hypervolemia found no neurological benefit. All four RCTs reported more pulmonary edema in hypervolemic arms; the observational study reporting that outcome found the same direction. A study comparing blood-volume-guided fluids in 54 patients with conventional care in 48 patients, whose clinical normovolemia target aimed at 750 mL positive daily fluid balance, found no DCI or other outcome difference and had critical bias risk. Comparison of computerized, hemodynamically guided fluid limitation with historical conventional care found fewer hypoxemic patients but no other outcome differences. Shikata et al. associated optimized, restricted fluid and sodium administration with better discharge mRS. Mutoh et al. randomized 160 patients between conventional care and an early goal-directed fluid therapy (EGDT) transpulmonary-thermodilution algorithm and found no significant pulmonary edema, DCI, or other outcome differences. Anetsberger et al. randomized 108 patients between standard care and a transpulmonary-thermodilution-based algorithm: daily intake and balance were similar, while the goal-directed group had less DCI and more favorable neurological outcomes at 3 months. Although some protocol studies suggested improvement, overall evidence was low to very low and supports no particular fluid or hemodynamic protocol. The panel recommends targeting euvolemia, while how best to assess or attain it remains undefined. Further study should address those techniques and noninvasive goal-directed approaches.

document_sections.heading: Hemodynamic Management: Blood Pressure and Cardiac Output Augmentation PICO Question
document_sections.content: This question evaluates blood pressure and/or cardiac output augmentation for patients at risk of, or diagnosed with, DCI against no augmentation, considering mortality, mRS, GOS, infarction, DCI prevention, pulmonary edema, myocardial infarction, and arrhythmia. Table 9 summarizes evidence. Data are insufficient to recommend for or against augmentation to prevent or treat DCI; given its risks, use should be cautious and individualized to hemodynamic status. Longstanding clinical use does not overcome the shortage of reliable supporting evidence, and the guidance does not evaluate particular drugs separately. Eight RCTs and four comparative observational studies were reviewed. Small samples and variation in patient selection, DCI definitions, complication reporting, and outcome assessment limited interpretation. Most interpretable studies found no benefit, and some associated augmentation with harm. Egge et al. found no DCI or GOS difference between prophylactic hypertensive hemodilution and normovolemia in Hunt and Hess grade I to III patients. Rondeau et al. found no angiographic-vasospasm difference between norepinephrine-induced hypertension and dobutamine-induced cardiac-index augmentation. In Togashi et al.'s two-by-two assessment of hypervolemia and induced hypertension, mRS did not differ, but induced-hypertension recipients had worse neurobehavioral scores and some serious adverse events, including pulmonary edema. Gathier et al.'s multicenter RCT of symptomatic DCI compared induced hypertension with normotension. Fluids and norepinephrine continued until deficits improved, systolic/mean arterial pressure reached a maximum of 230/130 mm Hg, or a complication arose. Slow recruitment ended the trial early; its authors noted more poor outcomes with induced hypertension. Of two RCTs examining monitored EGDT, one found no significant DCI or mRS difference, and the other associated invasive protocol-driven monitoring with less DCI and improved 3-month GOS but unchanged mortality. Studies comparing IV milrinone with IV+ IA milrinone or with continuous magnesium infusion for 21 days were inconclusive because of moderate to serious bias. Panel members considered existing studies too small and locally dependent to resolve the discrepancy between practice and findings; concomitant surgical and intensive-care interventions may also confound outcomes. Insufficient supportive research, rather than adequate studies definitively showing no benefit, underlies the inability to recommend either direction. Several studies associated augmentation with cardiovascular adverse events. Gathier et al. reported severe adverse events in 11% versus 5% with induced hypertension versus its comparator (Relative risk 2.1; 95% CI 0.9–5.0), including death, pneumothorax, atrial fibrillation, and myocardial infarction. Complications warrant close monitoring and individualized treatment. Whether augmentation reduces ischemic injury or improves function after DCI needs further study.

document_sections.heading: DCI Management: Triggers for Interventional Procedures for Treatment of DCI PICO Question
document_sections.content: The question compares intervention triggered by neurological-examination change plus advanced neuroimaging—Computed Tomography (CT) Angiography, CT Perfusion, or transcranial Doppler—with intervention triggered by examination change alone, assessing mortality, mRS, GOS, and new infarction. Table 10 shows the evidence profile. No studies directly compared these triggers, so evidence is insufficient to recommend the optimal approach or claim either is superior. Although centers commonly use formal or informal protocols and studies have identified clinical, imaging, or quantitative electroencephalogram predictors of DCI, those studies did not directly compare the specified intervention triggers. One imaging-and-clinical predictor study addressed baseline vasospasm prediction rather than selection for intervention as DCI developed. Another concerned severe aSAH and used neuroimaging in both compared arms. The panel identifies uncertainty and practice variation as reasons for urgent research. Cross-center descriptive and observational comparisons could characterize variation but carry high bias risk; a direct comparison or cluster randomized trial of at least two strategies, including one incorporating neuroimaging, is needed.

document_sections.heading: Mineralocorticoid Therapy for the Management of Hyponatremia PICO Question
document_sections.content: This question compares mineralocorticoids with no mineralocorticoids for mortality, mRS, GOS, new infarction, serum sodium, and fluid balance; Table 11 profiles the evidence. Evidence is insufficient to support their administration to preserve normal sodium, maintain even fluid balance, or improve function. Despite use after hyponatremia and polyuria develop, no study tested treatment of established hyponatremia: available studies examined prevention of hyponatremia and volume contraction. Whether correcting hyponatremia with these drugs improves function has not been formally evaluated. Four RCTs had high bias risk, particularly from absent blinding, and limited precision because they included between 28 and 91 patients. They evaluated fludrocortisone or hydrocortisone begun within 48–72 h of onset and continued for 10–14 days against no intervention or placebo. Primary outcomes varied and included hyponatremia, generally sodium lower than 135 mEq/L for at least 2 consecutive days, negative fluid balance, and negative sodium balance; functional outcomes and DCI were secondary. Findings suggested less hyponatremia and natriuresis without an effect on DCI or function, and hypokalemia was more common with mineralocorticoids. Evidence does not establish a functional benefit. Early treatment might lower hyponatremia incidence, but the available findings are inconclusive; larger, more rigorous prevention and treatment trials are needed.

document_sections.heading: Management of Anemia PICO Question
document_sections.content: The question contrasts an aggressive transfusion strategy maintaining hemoglobin > 10 g/dL with a conservative strategy maintaining > 7 g/dL, examining mortality, mRS, GOS, infarction, DCI prevention, and transfusion complications. Table 12 presents the evidence profile. Evidence is insufficient to recommend a transfusion threshold higher than hemoglobin > 7 g/dL in aSAH. Anemia is common and associated with poor functional outcome, making transfusion targets clinically relevant, but quality evidence for higher targets specifically in aSAH is scarce. The review identified one RCT, one nonrandomized observational study, and five outcome analyses. In a small safety-and-feasibility RCT, Naidech et al. compared hemoglobin goals of at least 10 g/dL and 11.5 g/dL instituted within 3 days of onset and found no differences in new infarction, DCI prevention, or transfusion-related complications. In a post hoc CONSCIOUS analysis, Ayling et al. used two propensity-score matching algorithms stratified by baseline hemoglobin; neither found a mortality-rate difference between matched patients. Optimal strategies, thresholds, and their effects on clinical outcomes remain unestablished, and further research is needed.

document_sections.heading: Management of Hydrocephalus PICO Question
document_sections.content: The question compares direct external ventricular drain (EVD) clamping with gradual weaning in aSAH patients with an EVD, assessing mortality, mRS, GOS, new infarction, ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement, infection, and drain complications. Table 13 profiles the evidence. Evidence is insufficient to recommend either EVD-removal strategy. Centers vary between the approaches when deciding whether removal is safe or VP shunting is needed, and comparisons have been inadequate. One RCT, one historical-control cohort study, and one multicenter observational study addressed the question. A single-center RCT randomized 81 patients to direct clamping or weaning over 3 days. VP shunting occurred in 63.4% with direct clamping versus 62.5% with gradual weaning; direct clamping shortened EVD use and intensive-care stay, while safety was comparable. A single-center observational comparison associated intermittent cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) drainage and rapid weaning with less VP shunting than continuous drainage and gradual weaning (13% vs. 35%), as well as shorter EVD, intensive-care, and hospital durations and fewer nonfunctioning drains. In a prospective multicenter study using a standardized protocol in 139 patients, adjusted analysis showed a nonsignificant trend toward less VP shunting with rapid versus gradual weaning (OR 0.43; 95% CI 0.18–1.03); rapid weaning was associated with fewer EVD days and nonfunctioning drains. VP shunt rates differed markedly between the single-center studies, a recurring limitation of this literature; the multicenter study standardized protocols to address it. Sparse findings appear to favor direct clamping, but determining the optimal strategy requires a large multicenter RCT with clearly specified weaning protocols and VP-shunt indications.

document_sections.heading: Summary
document_sections.content: Outcomes following aSAH have improved, but many management questions remain unanswered. This evidence-based guideline identifies interventions supported as beneficial, ineffective, or harmful and highlights priorities for research. Care is complex and still requires clinical judgment. Multiple drugs have undergone RCT testing, whereas evidence for nonpharmacological questions was consistently poor, partly because management algorithms involve many interacting components and possible pathways. Better-quality research will require collaboration among neurocritical-care and neurosurgical communities and funding agencies.
